Area Forecast Discussion
National Weather Service Pendleton OR
924 PM PST Fri Nov 27 2026

.KEY MESSAGES...
- Widespread rain and mountain snow today.

- Mountain snowfall above 4000-4500 ft (southern Washington) 
  and 4000-5500 ft (northeast Oregon) into tonight.

- Drier conditions return Saturday, followed by another low-
  pressure system and widespread precipitation chances Sunday
  and Monday.

&&

.DISCUSSION...
It's been another rainy day for the majority of our forecast 
area as an inland-penetrating atmospheric river event 
continues. Ample integrated vapor transport (IVT) in the range 
of 250-750 kg/(m*s) is advertised by ensemble guidance to remain
in place through this afternoon, with the highest amounts 
across northern Oregon and far southern Washington. A well- 
defined quasi-stationary front is already set up over northern 
Oregon, and we are still anticipating a weakly defined surface 
low to arrive from the Pacific later this afternoon, which
coupled with an incoming shortwave trough will help pull colder
air southward and facilitate lowering snow levels. Currently, 
north of the frontal boundary, snow levels are generally in the
4500-5000 ft range across the Washington Cascades which is too
high for accumulating snowfall for mountain passes. Lowering
snow levels this evening are still forecast to bring accumulating
snow in the 1-4" range for the White Pass area along US 12.
Confidence is highest in totals of 1-3" (80% confidence).

Farther south, some uncertainty remains in how low snow levels 
will fall this afternoon and evening across the mountain passes
over the northern Blue Mountains; this will affect how much 
winter weather is observed along Interstate 84 and OR 204. 
Currently, snow levels are too high (5000-5500 ft) to produce 
much accumulation for OR 204 given the marginal surface 
temperatures of 32-34 degrees. There is still a low chance 
(20-30%) that snow levels will drop to 4000-4500 ft for a 
sufficient period to facilitate a noteworthy snow event later 
this afternoon through this evening for OR 204 and limited
portions of Interstate 84. Have not issued any headlines today 
due to marginal confidence in reaching advisory thresholds (6 
inches) for any of the aforementioned mountain regions.

Along the front, noteworthy rainfall is ongoing for the lower 
elevations of north-central and northeast Oregon and southeast 
Washington; rainfall totals in the 0.25-0.50" range have already
fallen along the foothills of the northern Blue Mountains, with
lower totals observed elsewhere. Anticipating another 0.20-0.50"
for most of the lower elevation areas this afternoon through
this evening. Precipitation is then expected to taper off 
tonight into early Saturday as a shortwave trough from the 
Pacific exits to the east is then replaced by an upper-level 
ridge Saturday.

Overnight and again Saturday night, areas of fog are forecast to
develop due to recent precipitation and subsidence under the
upper-level ridge.

Ensemble guidance is showing another low-pressure system and a
period of active weather Sunday and Monday, and the NBM is  
painting widespread 60-95% PoPs over the forecast area Sunday 
afternoon into Sunday night. All clusters of QPF scenarios from
ensemble guidance suggest area-wide precipitation, with the
heaviest amounts along the Cascades. 

Drier conditions are then forecast going into the middle of the
week as ensemble clusters show another Pacific low diving south
of the region into California and the Southwest. The Pacific 
Northwest is favored to be under upper-level ridging or a split
flow during that period.

&&

.AVIATION /06Z TAFS THROUGH 06Z SUNDAY/...
MVFR to IFR conditions are observed with low VIS and CIGs
expected through the TAF period at most sites. Precipitation in
the area is already beginning to taper off, but the subsidence 
left behind by the inland atmospheric river will bring dense fog
and low VIS to all sites overnight through early tomorrow 
morning. RDM/BDN/YKM/PSC are expected to see VIS as low as a 
quarter mile tomorrow morning and CIGs less than 3000 feet 
through the morning and early afternoon. Conditions should begin
to improve through the afternoon tomorrow as an upper-level 
ridge is expected to bring drier conditions and calm weather. 
Ames/01
